title: The Invisible Heroes in Our Kitchens
hook: Meet the microbes that ferment our food, clean our water, and save lives — everyday science in your dahi.

slides.title: The Invisible Heroes in Our Kitchens
slides.storyContext: On a sunny morning at Rajesh's dairy farm in Ludhiana, Priya arrives to study how microbes make yogurt. Ammachi joins via video call from Kerala.

image.alt: The Invisible Heroes in Our Kitchens — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Why Dahi Tastes Like Home
slides.storyContext: Rajesh shows Priya how the milk from his cows is kept warm overnight. 'Magic happens here,' he says. Ammachi explains: 'In my time, we called it sour milk. Now we know — it's Lactobacillus lactis eating the lactose and making lactic acid.' Priya pulls out her phone: 'And that acid curdles the milk into yogurt. The same bacteria lives in our gut!'

image.alt: Why Dahi Tastes Like Home — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: What are Microbes? The Microscopic Kingdom
slides.storyContext: Priya opens her laptop and shows images of bacteria, fungi, and archaea under a microscope. 'We're surrounded by trillions of organisms we can't see. Most are harmless; many are helpful. They're everywhere — in our food, our bodies, our soil.'

points.label: Bacteria
points.text: Prokaryotic; no nucleus; typically 0.5–5 μm; reproduce by binary fission. Can be spherical (cocci), rod-shaped (bacilli), or spiral (spirilla). Many have flagella for movement.

points.label: Fungi
points.text: Eukaryotic; cell wall of chitin; reproduce via spores. Include yeasts (unicellular) and molds (filamentous). Decomposers; some are pathogens, many are useful (fermentation, antibiotics).

points.label: Archaea
points.text: Prokaryotic but genetically distinct; thrive in extreme conditions (hot springs, salt marshes, deep ocean). Methanogens produce methane; halophiles tolerate high salt.

slides.inSimpleWords: Microbes are tiny living things: bacteria, fungi, and archaea. Most are invisible to the naked eye. They do the work of breaking down organic matter, making food, and even making medicine.

image.alt: What are Microbes? The Microscopic Kingdom — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Fermentation by Lactic Acid Bacteria
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a diagram: milk → glucose + lactose → pyruvate → lactic acid + energy (ATP). 'Lactobacillus has no mitochondria,' she explains, 'so it breaks down glucose without oxygen — anaerobic respiration.'

points.label: Lactic Acid Fermentation
points.text: Lactobacillus lactis converts milk sugar (lactose) into lactic acid (C₃H₆O₃), lowering pH from ~6.7 to ~4.6, causing casein protein to precipitate and form yogurt curd.

points.label: Industrial Scale
points.text: Dairies maintain 43°C (optimal for the bacteria) and use starter cultures — pure strains of Lactobacillus added to millions of liters daily.

points.label: Probiotic Benefits
points.text: Live Lactobacillus in yogurt aid digestion, produce B vitamins, and support gut health. Some strains (L. acidophilus, L. rhamnosus) reduce lactose intolerance and boost immunity.

example.problem: If 1 L of milk contains 45 g lactose and Lactobacillus converts 90% to lactic acid in 8 hours, how much lactic acid is produced (assuming 1 glucose → 2 lactic acid, and lactose = 2 glucose)?
example.solution: 45 g × 0.9 = 40.5 g lactose; lactose (MW 342) = 40.5/342 = 0.118 mol; yields 0.236 mol lactic acid ≈ 21.3 g.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria eat milk sugar in the dark and cold (no air) and spit out an acid that makes milk clump into yogurt.

image.alt: Fermentation by Lactic Acid Bacteria — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: The Science Behind Ammachi's Kitchen Secrets
slides.storyContext: Ammachi shows Priya jars of pickled mangoes, fermented cucumber, and idli batter steaming on the stove. 'Each has its own bacteria and time,' she says. 'Pickle ferments in salt for weeks; idli rises in one night because of different bacteria.'

image.alt: The Science Behind Ammachi's Kitchen Secrets — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Cheese & Fermented Foods Across India
slides.storyContext: Ammachi brings up paneer: 'We use acid (dahi or lemon) and heat to curdle milk. But true cheese — aged for months — has different bacteria. In the south, we ferment rice and lentils for idli using Bacillus; in the north, people ferment rice bran for navratan.'

points.label: Paneer (Acid-curdled)
points.text: Milk + citric/lactic acid → curd + whey. No bacterial fermentation; coagulation by acid alone. Ready in 30 min. Fresh, mild, used in curries.

points.label: Cheese (Bacterial Fermentation)
points.text: Curd + salt + Streptococcus/Lactobacillus strains → aged 3–12 months. Bacteria produce flavor compounds (esters, alcohols, volatile acids). Higher protein, longer shelf life.

points.label: Idli & Fermented Grains
points.text: Rice + urad dal soaked 4–8 hours; Bacillus subtilis & Leuconostoc mesenteroides ferment → CO₂ gas makes idli fluffy; lactic acid aids digestion and nutrient bioavailability.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different bacteria + different foods + different times = dahi, paneer, cheese, or idli. Each has bacteria specially suited.

image.alt: Cheese & Fermented Foods Across India — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Example: Fermentation Kinetics in Idli Batter
slides.storyContext: Priya measures the pH of idli batter every 2 hours during fermentation. The bacteria produce acid steadily; the batter rises in volume as CO₂ accumulates.

example.problem: Idli batter (rice + urad dal) is inoculated with Bacillus subtilis. Initial pH = 6.5. After fermentation, lactic acid accumulates at 0.8 g/L per hour. Isoelectric point of proteins in batter ≈ pH 4.6. (a) How many hours until pH reaches 4.6? (b) What volume of CO₂ (at STP) is produced from 1 kg batter (assume 50 g carbohydrates ferment to lactic acid + CO₂, 1:1 molar ratio)?
example.solution: (a) Assume linear pH drop: Δ[lactic acid] needed ≈ 20 mmol/L (from pH 6.5 to 4.6, assuming buffering capacity). At 0.8 g/L per hour (MW lactic acid = 90): 0.8/90 = 8.9 mmol/L per hour. Time ≈ 20/8.9 ≈ 2.2–2.5 hours (idli fermentation is typically 4–8 hours, so other factors limit; temperature, inoculum size affect kinetics). (b) Carbohydrates (50 g) = 50/180 ≈ 0.278 mol glucose. Fermentation: 1 glucose → 1 lactic acid + 1 ethanol or CO₂ (simplified). CO₂ ≈ 0.278 mol × 22.4 L/mol ≈ 6.2 L CO₂ per kg, producing visible rise.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria in the batter eat starch, produce acid (making it sour) and gas (making it puffy). As hours pass, the batter becomes lighter and airier.

slides.title: Biogas: Methanogens Turning Waste to Energy
slides.storyContext: Rajesh points to a biogas digester on his farm — a sealed tank fed with cow dung. 'My electricity bill dropped 40%,' he says. Priya explains: 'Anaerobic bacteria — especially Methanococcus — break down organic matter in stages and produce methane gas.'

points.label: Methanogenesis (4 Stages)
points.text: 1. Hydrolysis (polymers → monomers), 2. Acidogenesis (fermentation → short-chain acids), 3. Acetogenesis (acids → acetate + H₂ + CO₂), 4. Methanogenesis (Archaea: acetate/H₂+CO₂ → CH₄).

points.label: Biogas Composition
points.text: 55–70% CH₄ (methane), 25–40% CO₂, <5% H₂S, N₂, O₂. Energy content ≈ 21.5 MJ/m³. Equivalent to ~0.6 L LPG or 0.5 kg coal per m³.

points.label: Inputs & Outputs
points.text: Cow dung (1 kg wet) → 30–40 L biogas. Digester residue = nitrogen-rich fertilizer (5x better than raw dung). Sustainable circular farming.

example.problem: A biogas digester fed 100 kg cow dung per day produces 3.5 m³ biogas at 60% CH₄. If cooking requires 2 MJ/meal and methane has 21.5 MJ/m³, how many meals can this system support daily?
example.solution: Methane volume = 3.5 × 0.6 = 2.1 m³; energy = 2.1 × 21.5 = 45.15 MJ; meals = 45.15 / 2 ≈ 22–23 meals/day.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria in sealed tanks eat dung in the dark and make a gas (methane) that burns like cooking gas.

image.alt: Biogas: Methanogens Turning Waste to Energy — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: A Farmer's Energy Independence
slides.storyContext: Rajesh walks Priya around his digester. 'In winter, when I can't work the fields, the digester keeps cooking. The leftover sludge enriches my soil. No chemical fertilizers, no electricity bills — the microbes do it all.' Priya nods: 'Closing a circle. Nothing wasted.'

image.alt: A Farmer's Energy Independence — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Challenge: Scale a Biogas System for a Dairy Village
slides.storyContext: Rajesh's village wants to build a community biogas plant to serve 50 small farms (each producing ~200 kg dung/day).

points.text: Calculate total daily dung input and expected daily biogas production (assume 35 L/kg dung, 65% CH₄).
How many cooking meals can this system support (2 MJ/meal, 21.5 MJ/m³ CH₄)?
Design the digester: what size tank (in m³) is needed for a 20-day retention time?

example.problem: Design the community biogas system.
example.solution: Daily dung: 50 × 200 = 10,000 kg. Biogas: 10,000 × 35/1000 = 350 m³/day. Methane: 350 × 0.65 = 227.5 m³. Energy: 227.5 × 21.5 = 4,891 MJ/day. Meals: 4,891 / 2 ≈ 2,445 meals/day. Tank size (20-day retention): 10,000 kg × 20 days = 200,000 kg = ~200 m³ at ~1 kg/L (slurry density). Recommend a 200–250 m³ digester (cylindrical, 10 m diameter × 2.5 m depth).

slides.inSimpleWords: Scale the single digester design to serve a whole village. Estimate biogas, energy, and digester size needed.

image.alt: Challenge: Scale a Biogas System for a Dairy Village — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Pathogenic Microbes & Disease Prevention
slides.storyContext: Priya reminds the class: 'Not all microbes are helpful. Salmonella poisons food. Mycobacterium causes TB. Our immune system and antibiotics fight them. But we must use antibiotics wisely — resistance is rising.'

points.label: Pathogenesis
points.text: Pathogenic bacteria produce toxins or invade tissues. Virulence factors: adhesins (stick to cells), invasins (penetrate), and toxins (damage). Examples: Vibrio cholerae (enterotoxin), Streptococcus pyogenes (M protein).

points.label: Antibiotic Resistance
points.text: Overuse of antibiotics selects for resistant mutants. Mechanisms: β-lactamase (breaks penicillin), altered ribosome (resists tetracycline), efflux pumps. Multi-drug resistant (MDR) bacteria increasingly common.

points.label: Prevention Strategies
points.text: Hygiene, vaccines, and judicious antibiotic use (complete courses, never self-prescribe). New antibiotics and alternatives (phage therapy, probiotics) being researched.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bad microbes cause disease. We fight them with hygiene, vaccines, and antibiotics. But overuse makes them resistant. Prevention is smarter than treatment.

image.alt: Pathogenic Microbes & Disease Prevention — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: The COVID-19 Wake-up Call
slides.storyContext: Priya reflects on 2020: 'A virus — not even alive, just RNA in a protein shell — shut down the world. We didn't have a vaccine. But biotechnology delivered one in a year (mRNA vaccines). Microbes can harm us, but tools to fight them can save us.'

image.alt: The COVID-19 Wake-up Call — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Antibiotics from Microbes: Penicillin & Beyond
slides.storyContext: Priya shows a photo of the Pfizer plant in India: 'Streptomyces bacteria secrete penicillin — a chemical that kills other bacteria by breaking their cell walls. Fleming discovered it by accident in 1928 when a mold contaminated his culture plate.'

points.label: Beta-Lactam Antibiotics
points.text: Penicillin (from Penicillium notatum) & Cephalosporin (from Streptomyces) inhibit bacterial peptidoglycan cross-linking → cell wall rupture → bacterial death.

points.label: Streptomycin from Soil
points.text: Streptomyces griseus produces streptomycin, binding to 30S ribosome → stops bacterial protein synthesis. Effective against TB (Mycobacterium tuberculosis).

points.label: Fermentation Scale
points.text: 1 L fermentation broth yields ~200–500 mg penicillin. Scaled to 10,000–100,000 L bioreactors; purification via chromatography.

slides.inSimpleWords: A mold or soil bacterium produces a poison that kills germs. We grow these microbes in huge tanks to make medicine.

image.alt: Antibiotics from Microbes: Penicillin & Beyond — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Fleming's Discovery: Accident That Saved Millions
slides.storyContext: Priya recounts the history to the village doctors: 'Fleming forgot a petri dish on his desk for a week. A mold grew on it and killed all the bacteria around it. He looked closer — and saw the future of medicine.' A doctor nods: 'Penicillin has saved countless lives from infections that once meant death.'

image.alt: Fleming's Discovery: Accident That Saved Millions — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Example: Antibiotic Production Scaling
slides.storyContext: A pharmaceutical company decides to increase penicillin output from 10 L to 1,000 L fermentation scale.

example.problem: A 10 L batch of Penicillium notatum fermentation yields 4 g penicillin (MW 334 Da) at harvest. Scaling to 1,000 L: (a) How much penicillin (in grams) would be expected if yield per volume is constant? (b) Assuming extraction efficiency is 85%, how many grams of purified penicillin are obtained? (c) At ₹2,000/gram market price, what is the revenue?
example.solution: (a) Scale factor: 1,000 / 10 = 100; expected penicillin = 4 × 100 = 400 g. (b) Purified: 400 × 0.85 = 340 g. (c) Revenue = 340 × ₹2,000 = ₹680,000 per batch. With 4–6 batches/year, annual revenue ≈ ₹2.7–4 million (before costs).

slides.inSimpleWords: As you grow more bacteria, you make more antibiotic. A small lab discovery scales to factory-level medicine production.

image.alt: Example: Antibiotic Production Scaling — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Wastewater & Environmental Microbes
slides.storyContext: In Kerala, Ammachi's village installed a constructed wetland system. 'The plants and microbes filter our water,' the engineer explained. Priya adds: 'Bacteria oxidize ammonia to nitrite, then nitrate (nitrification); others break down organic matter (heterotrophic bacteria); fungi & protozoa graze on bacteria to control population.'

points.label: Nitrification
points.text: Nitrosomonas oxidizes NH₃ → NO₂⁻; Nitrobacter oxidizes NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻. Aerobic; removes nitrogen from wastewater. Requires dissolved oxygen ≥2 mg/L.

points.label: Heterotrophic Oxidation
points.text: Bacteria (e.g., Pseudomonas) oxidize organic carbon (BOD) → CO₂ + H₂O using O₂. Reduces biochemical oxygen demand. Typical BOD removal rate: 1–3 g/m³/day.

points.label: Constructed Wetlands
points.text: Plants (reeds, cattails) + biofilm bacteria on substrate + protozoa. Low-tech, energy-efficient; treats sewage to near-potable levels. Removes 80–95% of BOD, 50–90% of nutrients.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria and plants together clean dirty water by eating the pollution and turning it into harmless gas or fertilizer.

image.alt: Wastewater & Environmental Microbes — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Clean Water from Microbes: A Village Transformed
slides.storyContext: Ammachi shows Priya the wetland after a year. 'Before, our water stank and made children sick. Now look — it's clear, fish live here, and the river downstream is cleaner too.' Priya smiles: 'Invisible heroes again, Ammachi.'

image.alt: Clean Water from Microbes: A Village Transformed — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Wastewater Treatment System
slides.storyContext: A textile factory in Tamil Nadu produces 100,000 L wastewater daily with 5,000 mg/L BOD and 800 mg/L NH₃. Design a treatment using microbial processes.

points.text: What are the microbes needed for BOD reduction and nitrification?
If an aerated basin achieves 90% BOD reduction, what is the final BOD (mg/L)?
Calculate the oxygen (O₂) demand for oxidizing the BOD (assume 1 g BOD ≈ 1.5 g O₂ required).

example.problem: Design a two-stage system: aerobic (BOD removal) + nitrification (ammonia removal).
example.solution: Stage 1: Aerated basin, 8–12 hour retention. Heterotrophic bacteria (Pseudomonas, Bacillus) oxidize BOD: 5,000 × 0.9 = 4,500 mg/L removed; final ≈ 500 mg/L. O₂ demand ≈ 4,500 × 1.5 / 1,000 = 6.75 g O₂ per liter of wastewater, or 675 kg O₂/day for 100 m³. Stage 2: Nitrification basin, 12–16 hour retention. Nitrosomonas + Nitrobacter oxidize NH₃: 800 mg/L → ~50 mg/L (90% removal). Additional aeration needed. Final effluent: BOD ~500 mg/L, NH₃ ~50 mg/L (acceptable for river discharge or reuse).

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine two bacterial processes to clean wastewater: first eat the organic matter, then convert ammonia to nitrate.

image.alt: Challenge: Design a Wastewater Treatment System — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Full Example: Industrial Yogurt Production
slides.storyContext: Rajesh decides to scale up. He buys a 500 L batch-fermentation tank, inoculates with Lactobacillus lactis starter, and maintains 43°C for 6 hours.

example.problem: 500 L milk (4.5% lactose) is inoculated with 2% (v/v) starter culture and fermented at 43°C. Lactobacillus lactis (generation time ≈ 22 min at 43°C) converts 85% of lactose to lactic acid in 6 hours. (a) How many generations occur? (b) What is the final lactic acid concentration (g/L)? (c) At what time is pH likely ≤ 4.6?
example.solution: (a) 6 hours = 360 min; 360/22 ≈ 16.4 generations. (b) Lactose: 500 L × 0.045 kg/L = 22.5 kg; 85% converted = 19.125 kg. Assuming ~1:1 lactose → lactic acid (stoichiometric simplification for fermentation): ≈ 19 g/L lactic acid. (c) At ~4.5 g/L lactic acid (pH ≈ 4.6), approximately 1.2–1.5 hours; but buffering in milk delays; typically reached in 4–5 hours under these conditions.

image.alt: Full Example: Industrial Yogurt Production — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Microbe-Based Solution for a Dairy
slides.storyContext: A dairy in Maharashtra produces 50,000 L wastewater daily. Your task: design a biogas digester + wastewater treatment system using microbial processes.

points.text: What microbes would you use for biogas production and what are their roles?
How would you integrate nitrification to remove ammonia from the waste?
If each liter of wastewater has 2,000 mg/L BOD, and heterotrophic bacteria reduce it by 90% in an aerated basin, what is the final BOD?

example.problem: Design the integrated system.
example.solution: Stage 1: Anaerobic digester (methanogens + acetogens) → biogas + digestate; ~30–40 day retention. Produces 1,500–2,000 m³/day biogas at 60% CH₄ (~150–200 kW equivalent). Stage 2: Aerobic basin with Pseudomonas/Bacillus → BOD reduction to ~200 mg/L (90% of 2,000). Stage 3: Nitrification tank (Nitrosomonas + Nitrobacter) → NH₃ to NO₃⁻. Final effluent: BOD ~200 mg/L, NH₃ ~50 mg/L. Revenue: biogas (~50 lakh rupees/year at current prices); cost savings on electricity and fertilizer (~1.5 crore/year operating savings).

image.alt: Challenge: Design a Microbe-Based Solution — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Enzyme Kinetics: How Bacteria Work at Different Speeds
slides.storyContext: Priya explains to Ammachi: 'Each microbe has a growth rate — a generation time. At optimal temperature, Lactobacillus divides every 22 minutes. But in cold water, it stops. In hot conditions, enzymes denature and cells die.'

points.label: Generation Time
points.text: Time for a bacterial cell to divide into two. Lactobacillus lactis: ~22 min at 43°C (optimal). Slower at lower temps; faster growth at warmer temps but limited by enzyme stability.

points.label: Enzyme Kinetics (Michaelis-Menten)
points.text: Vmax (max reaction velocity) and Km (substrate concentration at half-max velocity). Rate depends on enzyme concentration, substrate, pH, and temperature.

points.label: Practical Control
points.text: In fermentation, temperature, oxygen, and substrate feed rate are tuned to maximize production rate and efficiency.

slides.inSimpleWords: Microbes have a speed — a generation time. Temperature, nutrients, and pH all dial that speed up or down. Optimize them, and you accelerate production.

image.alt: Enzyme Kinetics: How Bacteria Work at Different Speeds — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Example: Batch Fermentation Kinetics
slides.storyContext: A biotech student models Lactobacillus growth in a jar over time: lag phase, exponential growth, stationary phase, decline.

example.problem: A batch fermentation starts with 10⁶ cells/mL Lactobacillus. Generation time = 22 min. Exponential phase lasts 5 hours. (a) How many cells/mL at end of exponential phase? (b) If stationary phase begins when nutrients are depleted (at ~10⁹ cells/mL), how long until stationary phase?
example.solution: (a) 5 hours = 300 min. Generations = 300/22 ≈ 13.6. Cells = 10⁶ × 2^13.6 ≈ 10⁶ × 12,000 ≈ 1.2 × 10¹⁰ cells/mL. (b) Stationary at 10⁹ cells/mL: 10⁶ × 2^n = 10⁹ → 2^n = 1,000 → n ≈ 10 generations ≈ 220 min ≈ 3.7 hours (rounded).

slides.inSimpleWords: Bacteria in a jar grow exponentially (doubling each generation) until nutrients run out. Then they plateau (stationary phase).

image.alt: Example: Batch Fermentation Kinetics — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Why Some Ferments Fail: The Microbe's Point of View
slides.storyContext: Priya watches Ammachi rescue a failed idli fermentation. 'Too cold. The bacteria couldn't work fast enough.' She teaches Priya: 'Each microbe is like a worker. If the temperature is wrong, the pH is wrong, or salt is too high, the worker refuses to work. Respect the microbe, and you get magic.'

image.alt: Why Some Ferments Fail: The Microbe's Point of View — Microbes in Human Welfare

slides.title: Challenge: Optimize Yogurt Fermentation for a Factory
slides.storyContext: A yogurt factory wants to reduce fermentation time from 6 hours to 4 hours while maintaining quality. Your task: determine optimal conditions.

points.text: Would increasing temperature from 43°C to 50°C speed up fermentation? What are the risks?
How would increasing starter culture concentration (from 2% to 5% inoculum) affect generation time?
Design an optimal fermentation profile: initial temp, inoculum size, time to target pH (4.6).

example.problem: Optimize for 4-hour fermentation.
example.solution: Option 1: Increase temp to 47–48°C (instead of 43°C), reducing generation time from 22 min to ~18 min. At 48°C: 4 hours = 240 min; ~240/18 ≈ 13.3 generations; robust growth but risk of denaturation if >50°C. Option 2: Increase inoculum to 3–5% v/v starter. More cells = faster total acid production (even if individual generation time unchanged). Combined: 47°C + 3% inoculum → fermentation in 4–4.5 hours. Final pH ≈ 4.6 achieved predictably. Quality: monitor titratable acidity and taste panel to ensure consistency.

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed up fermentation by increasing temperature (carefully) and starter culture. Each change has trade-offs in quality and predictability.

image.alt: Challenge: Optimize Yogurt Fermentation for a Factory — Microbes in Human Welfare

subject: Biology
title: Building Life with Genetic Scissors
hook: How scientists use enzymes and plasmids to copy DNA, cut genes, and paste them into new organisms — the tools of modern life design.

slides.title: Building Life with Genetic Scissors
slides.storyContext: Arjun visits Dr. Sharma's lab in Bangalore, where Meera is running a centrifuge. 'We are writing a new chapter in a cell's story today,' Dr. Sharma smiles.

image.alt: Building Life with Genetic Scissors — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: The Day We Rewrote Genes
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma shows Arjun a petri dish: 'This bacteria now glows under UV light. We inserted a gene from a jellyfish into its DNA.' Meera adds: 'We did it using restriction enzymes, plasmids, and ligase — molecular scissors, shuttles, and glue. Three tools, infinite possibilities.'

image.alt: The Day We Rewrote Genes — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: The Central Dogma: DNA → RNA → Protein
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma draws on the whiteboard: 'All life follows one basic rule: information flows from DNA to RNA to proteins. To clone a gene, we need to understand this flow and intercept it at key points.'

points.label: DNA
points.text: Double-stranded helix; permanent storage of genetic information. Replicates before cell division; bases pair A-T and G-C.

points.label: RNA
points.text: Single-stranded copy; transfers information from DNA to ribosomes. mRNA (messenger) carries genes; rRNA/tRNA (structural/functional).

points.label: Protein
points.text: Chains of amino acids; does the work. Three-letter genetic code (codons) on mRNA specify amino acids. Proteins fold into 3D structures.

slides.inSimpleWords: DNA is the instruction manual. RNA is a copy of the instructions. Proteins are what the instructions build. Biotechnology hijacks this process to read, copy, and rewrite instructions.

image.alt: The Central Dogma: DNA → RNA → Protein — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: DNA Replication: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction)
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma pulls up a thermal cycler on his laptop. 'PCR is a copying machine. We heat DNA to 94°C, cool to 55°C for primers to bind, then warm to 72°C so DNA polymerase copies. Repeat 30 times: 1 copy → 2^30 = over 1 billion copies in 3 hours.'

points.label: Three Phases Per Cycle
points.text: 1. Denaturation (94°C): double helix splits into single strands. 2. Annealing (50–65°C): short DNA primers bind to target sequence. 3. Extension (72°C): Taq polymerase adds nucleotides, copying the strand.

points.label: Taq DNA Polymerase
points.text: From thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus; stable up to 99°C; optimal 72°C. Doesn't have 3'→5' exonuclease (proofreading), so error rate ≈ 1 per 10,000 bases.

points.label: Amplification Formula
points.text: After n cycles: (number of DNA molecules) = initial DNA × 2^n. With 1 ng starting DNA and 35 cycles: ~34 μg final product.

example.problem: A PCR reaction starts with 10 copies of a target DNA segment. After 25 cycles, how many copies are present?
example.solution: Copies = 10 × 2^25 = 10 × 33,554,432 ≈ 335 million copies.

slides.inSimpleWords: A machine heats and cools DNA over 30+ cycles. Each cycle doubles the DNA. After one hour, you have a billion copies.

image.alt: DNA Replication: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: A Breakthrough Morning in the Lab
slides.storyContext: Meera arrives early and checks the PCR machine. 'Look at this gel from yesterday's run!' she tells Dr. Sharma, pointing to bright bands. 'The GFP gene amplified perfectly. We have trillions of copies now — enough for the entire cloning project.' Arjun leans in, fascinated. 'You started with a tiny speck of DNA?'

image.alt: A Breakthrough Morning in the Lab — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Restriction Enzymes & DNA Cutting
slides.storyContext: Meera points to a gel image: 'See these bands? We cut a DNA plasmid with EcoRI enzyme at specific sequences. Each cut site is recognized by a specific 6-bp sequence: GAATTC. The enzyme slices it like scissors through paper.'

points.label: Recognition & Cutting
points.text: Restriction endonuclease recognizes palindromic DNA sequences (e.g., GAATTC for EcoRI) and cuts between specific nucleotides, producing sticky ends (overhangs) or blunt ends.

points.label: Sticky vs. Blunt Ends
points.text: Sticky ends (e.g., EcoRI: 5'-G↓AATTC-3') are complementary; they easily ligate to other fragments cut by the same enzyme. Blunt ends (e.g., PvuII) are harder to ligate.

points.label: Restriction Maps
points.text: Cutting plasmid DNA with multiple enzymes produces fragments of known sizes; mapping cuts helps identify gene insertion sites and verify cloning success.

slides.inSimpleWords: A protein enzyme cuts DNA at a specific sequence (like GAATTC). Different enzymes cut at different sequences — this lets us open DNA at just the right place.

image.alt: Restriction Enzymes & DNA Cutting — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Example: Restriction Mapping a Plasmid
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma uses three restriction enzymes to cut a plasmid and create a map. The pattern of fragment sizes tells them where the cut sites are.

example.problem: A plasmid (3.5 kb total) is digested with: (a) EcoRI alone → 3.5 kb (no cut, circular DNA remains intact). (b) BamHI alone → 3.5 kb. (c) EcoRI + BamHI → 2.0 kb + 1.5 kb fragments. (d) EcoRI + PstI → 2.1 kb + 1.4 kb. Where are the restriction sites?
example.solution: EcoRI and BamHI each cut once (produce single fragment from circular DNA). EcoRI + BamHI produces two fragments: sites are ~2.0 kb apart (EcoRI to BamHI clockwise) and ~1.5 kb apart (BamHI to EcoRI clockwise). PstI is 1.4 kb from EcoRI (in one direction) and 2.1 kb in the other. This maps out a restriction map and confirms plasmid structure.

slides.inSimpleWords: By cutting with different enzyme combinations and measuring fragment sizes, we create a map of where each enzyme cuts on the DNA.

image.alt: Example: Restriction Mapping a Plasmid — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: DNA Ligase & Plasmids: Pasting Genes
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma shows Arjun a plasmid diagram — a circular DNA from bacteria: 'Plasmids are natural gene carriers. We cut the plasmid with EcoRI, insert our jellyfish GFP gene (also cut with EcoRI), then add DNA ligase to seal the nicks.'

points.label: Plasmids
points.text: Extra-chromosomal circular DNA in bacteria; typically 5–50 kb; carries antibiotic-resistance genes, metabolic genes, or replication origins. Replicate independently of chromosome.

points.label: DNA Ligase (T4 Ligase)
points.text: Catalyzes phosphodiester bond formation between 3'-OH and 5'-phosphate ends (nick closure). Requires ATP. Seals single-strand breaks in double-stranded DNA.

points.label: Recombinant Plasmid
points.text: Plasmid + inserted foreign DNA (e.g., GFP gene) = recombinant plasmid. Must have selectable marker (e.g., ampicillin-resistance gene) and origin of replication.

slides.inSimpleWords: A plasmid is a tiny circular DNA loop bacteria use to share genes. We cut it open, glue in a new gene, seal it with ligase, and now the plasmid carries our gene.

image.alt: DNA Ligase & Plasmids: Pasting Genes — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Transformation: Getting DNA Into Cells
slides.storyContext: Meera dips bacteria into ice-cold CaCl₂ solution. 'This makes their membranes porous. When we heat-shock them, the recombinant plasmid slips inside. Not all bacteria take it up — maybe 1 in 1,000 — but we find them by antibiotic selection.'

points.label: Chemical Transformation (CaCl₂)
points.text: Competent cells (made permeable by Ca²⁺) are mixed with recombinant DNA, chilled, then heat-shocked (42°C, 90 sec). Plasmid enters cell during repair of heat-induced membrane stress. Efficiency: 10⁶–10⁹ transformants per microgram DNA.

points.label: Electroporation
points.text: High-voltage pulse (1–2.5 kV) creates transient pores in cell membrane, allowing DNA entry. Faster, higher efficiency. Works for many cell types (not just bacteria).

points.label: Selectable Markers
points.text: Recombinant plasmid carries antibiotic resistance (e.g., ampicillin-resistance gene). Only transformed cells survive on antibiotic-agar plates. Non-transformed cells die.

example.problem: A transformation yields 500 colonies on ampicillin plates from 100 ng recombinant plasmid. Calculate the transformation efficiency (colonies per microgram DNA).
example.solution: 500 colonies / (100 ng / 1000 ng/μg) = 500 / 0.1 = 5,000 colonies/μg. Efficiency = 5 × 10³ transformants/μg (a reasonable result for chemical competence).

slides.inSimpleWords: We make bacteria's walls soft with cold salt, sneak the plasmid inside with heat, then only bacteria carrying the plasmid survive on poison-laced food (antibiotics).

slides.title: Screening for Winners on the Agar Plate
slides.storyContext: The next morning, Arjun and Meera examine the antibiotic plates. 'These colonies should have the recombinant plasmid,' Meera says, pointing to white colonies on the blue-white plate. 'The blue bacteria have no insert, or a different insert. The white ones are our clones.' She picks three colonies for verification.

image.alt: Screening for Winners on the Agar Plate — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Blue-White Screening & Colony Selection
slides.storyContext: Meera explains lacZ complementation: 'The plasmid has a lacZ gene (encodes β-galactosidase, turns substrate blue). If we cut it and insert a gene, it breaks lacZ. So: blue = no insert, white = insert. Simple, visual.'

points.label: lacZ Complementation
points.text: β-galactosidase (from lacZ gene) cleaves X-gal substrate → blue color. If gene inserts into lacZ, enzyme is disrupted → white color. Rapid visual screen on one plate.

points.label: Selection vs. Screening
points.text: Selection: antibiotic kills non-transformed cells. Screening: blue-white identifies recombinants. Combined: 1st round (antibiotic agar) selects transformed; 2nd round (blue-white) identifies correct insert.

points.label: High-Throughput Alternatives
points.text: CRISPR/Cas selection: toxic counter-selection if insert absent. Barcode screening: sequencing barcodes in plasmid pool.

slides.inSimpleWords: Blue-white screening lets us see which bacteria have the insert we want. No insert = blue. Insert breaks the color gene = white. Pick white colonies.

image.alt: Blue-White Screening & Colony Selection — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Gel Electrophoresis: Seeing the DNA
slides.storyContext: Arjun watches Meera pour a gel and load samples. 'DNA is negatively charged. When we apply an electric field, it migrates through the gel toward the positive pole. Smaller fragments move faster.'

points.label: Separation by Size
points.text: Agarose gel (0.8–1.5% w/v) acts as a molecular sieve. DNA molecules migrate based on charge-to-mass ratio (all DNA has similar charge), so migration ≈ inverse of size. Smaller DNA: faster; larger DNA: slower.

points.label: EtBr Staining & Visualization
points.text: Ethidium bromide intercalates into double-stranded DNA; fluoresces orange under UV. Allows direct visualization. Fragment size is determined by comparing to a DNA ladder (standard markers of known sizes).

points.label: Applications
points.text: Verify PCR products, check restriction digestion, assess plasmid size, check for contaminating chromosomal DNA.

slides.inSimpleWords: DNA moves through a jelly-like gel when electricity pushes it. Small pieces run fast, big pieces run slow. We stain it orange and see the result under UV light.

image.alt: Gel Electrophoresis: Seeing the DNA — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Challenge: Verify a Recombinant Clone
slides.storyContext: Meera picks three colonies and grows them overnight. She extracts plasmid DNA and digests with EcoRI + BamHI to check if the insert is present.

points.text: What fragment sizes would you expect from (a) empty plasmid, (b) plasmid with insert?
If the original plasmid is 2.7 kb and the GFP insert is 1.2 kb, what sizes do you see on the gel for a successful clone?
Design a screening strategy: how would you identify the one clone with the GFP insert oriented correctly?

example.problem: Identify the correct clone.
example.solution: 1. Empty plasmid (2.7 kb) digested with EcoRI + BamHI (directional cloning, each cuts once): → 2.7 kb (uncut, or linearized if only one cut site). 2. Recombinant with insert: 2.7 + 1.2 = 3.9 kb total; digest → 2.7 kb vector + 1.2 kb insert (two fragments). 3. Gel: non-recombinant shows single 2.7 kb band; recombinant shows 2.7 + 1.2 kb. Pick colonies showing both bands. 4. Orientation verification: sequence the junction or use a different enzyme combination (e.g., EcoRI alone: if insert has no internal EcoRI, non-recombinant linearizes to 2.7 kb, recombinant stays at 3.9 kb due to internal cut and religation if insert is in correct orientation).

slides.inSimpleWords: Run a digest & gel to see if the plasmid has the insert. Different fragment patterns tell you success or failure.

image.alt: Challenge: Verify a Recombinant Clone — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Full Example: Cloning the GFP Gene
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma outlines the complete protocol: isolate GFP gene from jellyfish DNA, amplify by PCR, digest with EcoRI, ligate into pUC19 plasmid, transform into E. coli, and select on ampicillin agar.

example.problem: You have 50 μL of GFP PCR product (1.2 kb) and 20 μL of pUC19 plasmid (2.7 kb). You digest both with EcoRI for 1 hour at 37°C (2 units/μL, 1 hour needed for 100% cutting). (a) After restriction digest, how many moles of each are present? (b) For 1:3 molar ratio insert:plasmid, calculate volumes needed for the ligation mix (assume 1 μL total DNA). (c) Approximate ligation efficiency if 500 colonies grown from 1 ng recombinant DNA?
example.solution: (a) GFP: (1.2 kb) × (50 μL) ≈ 60 μg; at 650 Da/bp: 60 × 10⁶ ng / (1.2 × 10³ × 650) ≈ 77 pmol. pUC19: (2.7 kb) × (20 μL) ≈ 54 μg; 54 × 10⁶ / (2.7 × 10³ × 650) ≈ 31 pmol. (b) For 1:3 ratio: need 10 pmol insert : 30 pmol plasmid. Volumes: GFP = (10/77) × 50 ≈ 6.5 μL; pUC19 = (30/31) × 20 ≈ 19.4 μL (scaled to 1 μL total). (c) Efficiency = 500 colonies / (1 ng / 1000 ng/μg) = 500,000 transformants/μg (efficient).

image.alt: Full Example: Cloning the GFP Gene — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Expression Vectors & Protein Production
slides.storyContext: Dr. Sharma shows Arjun an expression plasmid diagram. 'This isn't just a shuttle for DNA. It has a promoter — a switch that turns the gene ON — and a terminator. Without these, the bacteria never read the gene. No protein is made.'

points.label: Promoter
points.text: DNA sequence recognized by RNA polymerase; initiates transcription. Strong promoters (e.g., T7) produce lots of mRNA. Inducible promoters (e.g., lac) turn on only when inducer (e.g., IPTG) is added.

points.label: Ribosome Binding Site (RBS)
points.text: Shine-Dalgarno sequence (bacteria) or Kozak sequence (eukaryotes). Positions ribosome at start codon (AUG). Affects translation efficiency; ~30–50% of expression variation.

points.label: Terminator & Purification Tags
points.text: Stop codon (TAG, TAA, TGA) ends translation. His-tag (6–10 His residues) binds Ni-NTA resin for easy purification. Tag is often removed later by protease cleavage.

slides.inSimpleWords: An expression vector is like a recipe card. It has a label (promoter), ingredients (gene), and instructions (terminator). RNA polymerase reads the label, ribosomes read the ingredients, and protein is made.

image.alt: Expression Vectors & Protein Production — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: The Art of Protein Purification
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Arjun a flask of brownish culture broth. 'This looks disgusting,' she laughs. 'But inside are billions of bacteria making insulin. Now we lyse them, denature, purify by column, and fold the chains together. One mistake, and it's ruined.'

image.alt: The Art of Protein Purification — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Example: Purification & Yield Calculation
slides.storyContext: After fermentation, protein is extracted, purified, and analyzed by SDS-PAGE (sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis) to check purity.

example.problem: A 1 L fermentation of E. coli expressing a 20 kDa protein yields 500 mL lysate. Lysate contains ~2 g/mL total protein. After Ni-NTA affinity chromatography, 100 mL eluate contains 10 mg/mL target protein (verified by SDS-PAGE). (a) Calculate yield (%). (b) Calculate purity (%).
example.solution: (a) Total protein in lysate: 500 mL × 2 g/mL = 1,000 g total. Target protein: 100 mL × 10 mg/mL = 1,000 mg = 1 g. Yield = 1 g / (1,000 g × expected % expression) ≈ assume 30% expression in lysate; true yield ≈ 1 / 300 ≈ 0.33%. (b) Purity: target protein in eluate = 1 g. Contaminants ≈ 100 mL × (2 g/mL - 10 mg/mL) ≈ 100 × 1.99 ≈ 199 g (rough estimate; actual depends on specificity). Purity after affinity ≈ 1 / (1 + 0.2) ≈ 83% (typical for single-step purification).

slides.inSimpleWords: We measure how much protein we got and how pure it is. Yield tells us efficiency; purity tells us if contaminants are present.

image.alt: Example: Purification & Yield Calculation — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Challenge: Troubleshoot a Failed Cloning
slides.storyContext: Arjun picked three colonies that grew on ampicillin plates. But the gel shows no insert — all three are empty vector.

points.text: What went wrong: was it ligation, transformation, or selection?
How would you verify each step (PCR, digestion, ligation efficiency)?
Design a new cloning with controls: what would a successful result look like on a gel?

example.problem: Troubleshoot the cloning failure.
example.solution: Likely culprrit: (1) PCR product was empty or wrong size (run PCR product on gel first). (2) Ligation efficiency was too low (too much DNA, not enough ligase, or short incubation). (3) Transformation was inefficient (controls: no plasmid, no insert). Fixes: (a) Re-PCR with fresh template + primers. (b) Re-ligation with 1:3 insert:plasmid molar ratio, T4 ligase (3 units/μg DNA), 4°C overnight. (c) Transform into fresh competent cells; run positive control (known insert). Expected gel: non-recombinant (empty) = linearized vector (2.7 kb); recombinant = 2.7 + 1.2 = 3.9 kb (two fragments after digest).

slides.inSimpleWords: When cloning fails, the issue is usually ligation or transformation. Test each step with controls and be systematic.

image.alt: Challenge: Troubleshoot a Failed Cloning — Biotechnology - Principles and Processes

slides.title: Challenge: Design an Insulin-Producing E. coli
slides.storyContext: A pharma company wants to produce recombinant human insulin in E. coli. Design the cloning strategy: identify the gene, PCR strategy, enzyme choice, plasmid features, and selection.

points.text: Where would you get the human insulin gene and what would you amplify by PCR?
Which restriction enzyme(s) and why? (Hint: consider sticky-end compatibility.)
What features must the expression plasmid have (promoter, terminator, marker)? Why?
How would you screen for successfully transformed colonies?

example.problem: Design the cloning strategy.
example.solution: 1. Source: Human cDNA library or synthesized gene (NCBI GenBank: insulin gene mRNA, 333 bp coding sequence). 2. PCR: primers add EcoRI + BamHI sites; amplify full-length insulin cDNA including start codon. 3. Digest both PCR product & plasmid (pET28a or similar expression plasmid) with EcoRI + BamHI (directional cloning). 4. Plasmid requirements: T7 promoter (strong constitutive/inducible), His-tag (purification), antibiotic marker (ampicillin), ori (replication). 5. Screen: 1° with antibiotic agar (ampicillin); 2° with blue-white screening (lacZ if available) or restriction digest of colonies; 3° with SDS-PAGE after IPTG induction to confirm 5.8 kDa insulin band.

points.label: Restriction Enzymes & Ligase

points.text: Circular bacterial DNA carries genes into cells; selectable markers identify successful transformants.

slides.storyContext: Three lives changed by biotechnology: Suresh's cotton crop, a diabetic patient's insulin, and a murder case solved by DNA. All on the same Sunday.

slides.title: Three Stories of Biotechnology
slides.storyContext: Suresh scrolls through his phone: 'My Bt cotton yields 50% more and needs half the pesticides. My margin went from ₹5,000/acre to ₹15,000.' Dr. Patel injects a diabetic patient with recombinant human insulin (rHI), made in E. coli: 'Twenty years ago, we extracted it from pig pancreases. Now we grow it in bacteria.' Anjali runs a DNA profile through the database: 'The hair from the crime scene matches the suspect 1 in 6.4 billion. Justice.'

slides.title: What is a Genetically Modified Organism (GMO)?
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel explains to Suresh: 'A GMO is an organism whose DNA has been deliberately altered using molecular biology techniques. A gene from one species is inserted into another, giving it new traits — like resistance to insects or herbicides.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: Organism with one or more genes from a different species. Gene is usually introduced via plasmid (bacteria) or gene gun (plants).

points.label: Trait Selection
points.text: Inserted genes must be selectable and heritable. Examples: insect resistance (Bt), herbicide tolerance (RoundUp Ready), drought resistance, enhanced nutrition.

points.label: Testing & Approval
points.text: Extensive testing for agronomic performance, toxicity, allergenicity, environmental impact. Requires regulatory approval (GEAC in India, EFSA in EU, FDA in US).

slides.inSimpleWords: Scientists take a useful gene from one organism and put it into another using biotechnology. The new organism has abilities it didn't have before.

image.alt: What is a Genetically Modified Organism (GMO)? — Biotechnology and its Applications

slides.title: Bt Cotton & Transgenic Crops
slides.storyContext: Suresh explains: 'The Bt gene comes from soil bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. It codes for a protein that kills the cotton bollworm caterpillar.' A biotech engineer inserted this gene into cotton DNA using Agrobacterium tumefaciens — a natural gene-transfer agent.

points.label: Bt Toxin Mechanism
points.text: Cry1Ac protein (from B. thuringiensis) forms pores in the midgut epithelium of lepidopteran larvae (bollworms, armyworms); causes cell lysis & death. Protein is not toxic to vertebrates (gut pH too high, no specific receptors).

points.label: Agrobacterium tumefaciens (Natural Gene Gun)
points.text: Plant pathogen naturally transfers DNA (T-DNA) into plant cells. Scientists removed disease genes, replaced with desired genes (Bt + selectable marker). Agrobacterium infects cotton embryos; T-DNA integrates into plant genome.

points.label: Advantages of Bt Crops
points.text: 50–90% pest loss reduction; 50–80% reduction in synthetic pesticide use; yield increase 10–40%; cost savings outweigh premium seed cost in 2–3 years.

example.problem: Bt cotton in India (avg. adoption ≥2004): 97% of cotton area by 2022. Assume average yield lift = 25%, pesticide cost reduction = 60%, and 10 million hectares cultivated. If pre-Bt yield = 15 bales/hectare and cotton market price = ₹5,000/bale, calculate the annual economic benefit for Indian farmers.
example.solution: Yield gain per hectare: 15 × 0.25 = 3.75 bales; market value = 3.75 × ₹5,000 = ₹18,750/ha. Pesticide savings (assume ₹3,000/ha baseline): 0.6 × ₹3,000 = ₹1,800/ha. Total benefit per hectare ≈ ₹20,550. Annual benefit = 10 million ha × ₹20,550 ≈ ₹205.5 billion (~$2.5 billion USD at 2022 rates).

slides.inSimpleWords: Scientists copied a poison gene from a bacterium into cotton DNA. The cotton plant now makes a poison that kills only caterpillars, not humans. Farmers spray less poison, earn more money.

image.alt: Bt Cotton & Transgenic Crops — Biotechnology and its Applications

slides.title: How Suresh's Farm Became a Success Story
slides.storyContext: A decade ago, Suresh was struggling. Pesticide costs soared, and pink bollworms decimated his crop. Then, in 2004, Bt cotton arrived in India. 'It wasn't magic,' Suresh recalls. 'But it came close. I stopped losing 30% of my crop to insects. I sprayed less poison, my kids' water was cleaner, and I actually earned enough to pay off my loans.'

slides.title: Recombinant Insulin: From Pigs to Bacteria
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel shows a vial of rHI. 'Before 1983, diabetics depended on insulin extracted from pig & cow pancreases — slow, expensive, impure, and risky of animal disease transfer. Now, Eli Lilly produces ≥100 tons/year of human insulin in E. coli.'

points.label: Gene Synthesis
points.text: Human insulin gene (51 aa A-chain, 30 aa B-chain, linked by disulfide bonds) is reverse-transcribed from mRNA, synthesized, and codon-optimized for E. coli (prefers certain codons).

points.label: Separate Chain Expression
points.text: A-chain and B-chain are expressed separately in E. coli as inclusion bodies (protein precipitate in cytoplasm). Extracted, denatured, then refolded in vitro with precise redox conditions to form disulfide bonds.

points.label: Disulfide Bond Formation
points.text: Insulin stability depends on 3 disulfide bonds: 2 inter-chain (A7-B7, A20-B19), 1 intra-chain (A6-A11). Refolding is a chemical-engineering challenge; yield ≈ 50–70%.

example.problem: A fermentation produces 2 g/L recombinant A-chain (MW 2,534 Da) and 1.5 g/L B-chain (MW 3,496 Da) in 10 L broth. After extraction & disulfide-bonding, assuming 60% yield, how much mature insulin (MW 5,808 Da) is produced?
example.solution: Moles A-chain: (2 × 10) / 2,534 = 0.00789 mol; moles B-chain: (1.5 × 10) / 3,496 = 0.00429 mol. Limiting reagent: B-chain (fewer moles). Insulin formed: 0.00429 mol × 5,808 Da × 60% = 15.0 g (roughly 1.5 g/L culture, a typical industrial titer).

slides.inSimpleWords: Scientists copied the human insulin gene into bacteria. The bacteria make two chains; we chemically link them, and voila — human insulin made in factory vats instead of pig pancreases.

slides.title: A Patient's Second Chance
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel describes his patient: a 12-year-old with Type 1 diabetes who once faced expensive animal-derived insulin. 'Now she injects recombinant insulin made in a bioreactor in Bangalore — pure, affordable, and she doesn't worry if it came from a pig. Her blood sugars are stable, and she can focus on being a child.'

slides.title: Genome Sequencing & Personalized Medicine
slides.storyContext: A patient with cancer gets their tumor DNA sequenced. Dr. Patel explains: 'We find the mutations driving their cancer, then recommend targeted drugs or immunotherapy. In 2010, a human genome took 10 years & $3 billion. Today, ₹20,000 & 3 days.'

points.label: DNA Sequencing Tech
points.text: Sanger sequencing (1977, ~1 kb/day, ₹1,000–2,000 per sample). Next-gen sequencing (NGS; 2007+, >100 Mb/day, ₹500–5,000 per genome). Third-gen (long reads, epigenetics). Nanopore (real-time, portable).

points.label: Tumor Profiling
points.text: Cancer mutations (point mutations, copy-number variations, structural variants) in driver genes (TP53, BRCA1/2, EGFR, etc.) guide therapy. Example: EGFR+ lung cancers respond to erlotinib; KRAS+ pancreatic cancers benefit from KRAS inhibitors.

points.label: Pharmacogenomics
points.text: Variant alleles in drug-metabolizing genes (CYP450, TPMT, etc.) predict drug response & toxicity. Warfarin dosing guided by CYP2C9 & VKORC1 genotypes; thiopurine metabolism by TPMT status.

slides.inSimpleWords: We read the DNA instructions in a patient's cancer or blood, spot the mistakes, and pick medicines that fix those specific mistakes.

image.alt: Genome Sequencing & Personalized Medicine — Biotechnology and its Applications

slides.title: Forensic DNA Profiling
slides.storyContext: Anjali runs a gel with DNA samples from the crime scene and three suspects. 'We look at short tandem repeats — STRs — microsatellites of 2–6 bp repeated many times. No two people (except identical twins) have the same STR pattern at 13+ loci.'

points.label: STRs (Short Tandem Repeats)
points.text: Repetitive sequences, e.g., GATA repeated 5–15 times. Each person inherits two alleles (one per parent). Variation in repeat count is common (polymorphic). 13 loci (FBI standard) = 2^13 = 8,192 combinations per locus.

points.label: Probability Calculation
points.text: Assuming independent loci, probability that a random person matches = product of allele frequencies. For 13 loci with typical diversity: ~1 in 6–10 billion. Indian population: ~1.4 billion, so match is virtually certain (identity).

points.label: DNA Extraction Sources
points.text: Blood (easiest), saliva (swabs), hair (root bulb), semen, skin cells (touch DNA). PCR amplifies STRs; capillary electrophoresis sizes fragments & counts repeats.

example.problem: A crime scene hair sample and a suspect's blood are profiled at 13 STR loci. At locus D3S1358, the hair has 15/16 repeats; the suspect has 15/17 repeats. Are they a match?
example.solution: No. At one locus, they differ (16 vs. 17 alleles). For a match, all 13 loci must match (both alleles must be identical at each locus). This single mismatch excludes the suspect with 100% certainty. (Note: If ≥11 of 13 match, and other evidence is strong, degradation or mixture may be suspected, but a clear mismatch rules out individual identity.)

slides.inSimpleWords: Each person has a unique genetic barcode (STRs). We copy these 13 tiny regions using PCR, measure their sizes, and create a profile. If all 13 match, it's the same person (1 in billions).

slides.storyContext: Anjali describes a cold case from five years ago: 'A young woman was assaulted, and the case went nowhere — no leads, no suspects. But the hair found at the scene remained in evidence. Last month, DNA from that hair matched a new suspect entered into the database. His conviction is coming. Science gave her justice.'

slides.title: Ethical Issues in Biotechnology
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel and Anjali debate over tea: 'CRISPR can cure disease, but should we edit embryos for intelligence or looks? GMOs feed billions, but who profits — farmers or corporations? DNA databases solve crimes, but what about privacy?'

points.label: Germline Editing Ethics
points.text: Editing embryos (germline) raises concerns: unknown off-target effects, consent issues (child can't consent to permanent changes), inequitable access (only wealthy). Somatic gene therapy (body cells only) is more accepted.

points.label: GMO & Intellectual Property
points.text: Bt cotton patent holders (Monsanto/Bayer) charge premium seed prices. Farmers prohibited from saving seed (Terminator technology). Controversy: technology benefits corporations, not small farmers.

points.label: DNA Privacy & Surveillance
points.text: DNA databases (CODIS in US, NDIS in India) solve crimes but raise privacy concerns. Genetic discrimination in insurance/employment possible. Regulation needed: who can access, how long data stored.

slides.inSimpleWords: Powerful tools can be misused. Society must decide: when is genetic editing okay? Who profits from GMOs? Should DNA be in databases? Science alone can't answer these questions.

image.alt: Ethical Issues in Biotechnology — Biotechnology and its Applications

slides.title: CRISPR-Cas9: Editing Genes
slides.storyContext: A biologist shows a diagram: 'CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) is a bacterial immune system. We hijack it to cut specific DNA sequences with nanometer precision. In 2020, two scientists won the Nobel Prize for CRISPR.'

points.label: CRISPR Components
points.text: Cas9 protein (endonuclease); guide RNA (sgRNA) designed to match target DNA. sgRNA binds Cas9 & directs it to cut DNA at PAM (protospacer adjacent motif, e.g., NGG for Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9).

points.label: Cutting & Repair
points.text: Cas9 cuts both DNA strands; cell's repair machinery (NHEJ) rejoins, often introducing errors (frameshift, knockout). Alternatively, HDR (homology-directed repair) inserts a template (for knock-in).

points.label: Clinical Potential
points.text: Sickle-cell disease (β-globin edit), β-thalassemia, cystic fibrosis (CFTR edit), some cancers (CAR-T via CRISPR edit). FDA approved exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy) for sickle-cell & β-thalassemia in Dec 2023.

slides.inSimpleWords: CRISPR is a molecular scissors that can find & cut a specific misspelled word in a 3-billion-letter genome. Cells repair the cut, usually disabling the bad gene or inserting a good one.

image.alt: CRISPR-Cas9: Editing Genes — Biotechnology and its Applications

slides.title: Full Example: Sickle-Cell Gene Therapy via CRISPR
slides.storyContext: A 14-year-old girl with sickle-cell disease undergoes CRISPR therapy: doctors extract her blood stem cells, edit the defective β-globin gene (or reactivate γ-globin), expand the cells in culture, and infuse them back.

example.problem: A patient's CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are edited via CRISPR: targeting BCOR6 (promotes γ-globin re-expression, compensating for β-globin defect). Assume: 5 × 10⁶ HSCs harvested, 85% transduction efficiency (CRISPR reaches the cell), 95% on-target editing (correct cut made), 5% off-target cuts at predicted sites. After expansion (20-fold), cells are reinfused. (a) How many edited cells are infused? (b) What safety concern arises from off-target cuts?
example.solution: (a) Edited cells: 5 × 10⁶ × 0.85 × 0.95 = 4.04 × 10⁶; after 20-fold expansion: 4.04 × 10⁶ × 20 = 80.8 × 10⁶ ≈ 81 million edited HSCs infused. (b) Off-target cuts at 5% of cells = 0.05 × 4.04 × 10⁶ ≈ 202,000 cells with unintended cuts. Risk: off-target cuts may disable tumor-suppressor genes (TP53, BRCA1) or activate oncogenes, raising long-term cancer risk. Monitoring via whole-genome sequencing and long-term follow-up required.

slides.title: Example: Estimating STR Match Probability
slides.storyContext: Anjali calculates the probability that a random person matches a crime-scene DNA profile.

example.problem: A crime-scene DNA profile is matched at 13 STR loci. Allele frequencies for each locus are known (typical population values). For example, locus 1 has alleles of size 10 and 12, with frequencies 0.05 and 0.03 in the population. Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium and independent loci: (a) Probability of this genotype at locus 1? (b) Probability of match at all 13 loci (with average frequency ~0.01 per genotype)?
example.solution: (a) Genotype (10, 12) = 2 × 0.05 × 0.03 = 0.003 (heterozygous frequency using 2pq formula). (b) If average probability per locus ≈ 0.001 (very rare), then match at 13 loci ≈ (0.001)^13 ≈ 10^-39. With population ~8 billion (8 × 10^9), probability of accidental match ≈ 0. Essentially certain match = identity.

slides.inSimpleWords: DNA profiles are so rare (1 in trillions) that a 13-locus match is virtually certain proof of identity.

slides.title: Challenge: Design a Gene Therapy for Muscular Dystrophy
slides.storyContext: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is caused by mutations in the 79-exon DMD gene (dystrophin protein, 3.6 million bp). Design a therapy using AAV (adeno-associated virus, 4.7 kb capacity, too small for full DMD) or CRISPR base-editing.

points.text: Why is DMD hard to treat with AAV (hint: gene size)?
How could microdystrophin (shortened, functional version, 2.2 kb) be delivered via AAV?
Alternatively, design a CRISPR base-editing strategy to correct a common nonsense mutation (UAG stop codon) in exon 50, restoring the reading frame.

example.problem: Design the therapy.
example.solution: 1. AAV Challenge: DMD gene is 3.6 Mb (>750× AAV capacity). Solution: deliver microdystrophin (2.2 kb) via AAV6.2 (muscle-tropic), driven by muscle-specific promoter (desmin). Targets 30–50% of muscle fibers; partial dystrophin restore improves function. 2. Base-Editing: nonsense mutation (exon 50, codon 1555, UAG) causes premature stop → truncated, non-functional dystrophin. Use ABE (adenine base editor) with guide RNA targeting the A in UAG. Base editor converts A→G (A:T pair → G:C), changing UAG (stop) → UGG (tryptophan). Result: full-length dystrophin re-expression. Deliver AAV-ABE + sgRNA; ~50–70% correction in transduced cells.
